personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Ron is defined by a distinctive cluster of traits: loyal and brave, but prone to insecurity about his place in a family of high-achievers; quick to defensiveness and sarcasm; fundamentally warm and funny; direct and unfiltered in his opinions. He is candidly self-deprecating about his family's poverty ('they couldn't aff-- I mean, I got Scabbers instead,' with pink ears) and his own status, yet he fights back fiercely when provoked (lunging at Malfoy for insulting his family, threatening Hermione with the Curse of the Bogies). His voice is marked by short, reactive sentences, casual humour ('throw it away and punch him on the nose'), bluntness ('she's a nightmare, honestly'), and periodic emotional outbursts. He is frequently wrong but rarely dishonest about himself. He shows genuine excitement and generosity (teaching Harry wizard chess, sharing his world with enthusiasm). Crucially, he carries constant low-grade anxiety about being overshadowed — Dumbledore confirms this is Ron's deepest desire when the Mirror shows him as head boy and Quidditch captain, 'the best of all of them.'
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves Ron's warmth, his loyalty, and his role as comic relief. His bluntness is intact: 'She's a nightmare, honestly. No wonder she hasn't got any friends,' delivered loud enough for Hermione to hear, matches the book tone precisely. His reactive humour is preserved ('Kill us faster?! Oh, now I can relax!'; 'Lucky we didn't panic'). His awe at Harry's fame is present but compressed. His defensiveness under pressure survives in the chess chamber. His sarcasm toward Hermione ('This is light?'; 'You do it then, if you're so clever') is well-rendered. His voice — short, reactive, emotionally immediate — is consistent throughout.
personality_voice.difference: Several secondary traits are reduced or missing. The book Ron's persistent, low-simmering insecurity about his family's poverty is almost entirely absent: the train scene cuts his halting self-correction about not being able to afford an owl, his embarrassment about hand-me-downs, and his gloomy comparison to his brothers. These are not isolated moments — they are a repeated pattern across many scenes that builds a specific emotional texture. In the film, Ron's self-consciousness about poverty manifests only faintly (he refuses food from the trolley). His competitive envy ('A Nimbus Two Thousand! I've never even touched one'; 'Ron moaned enviously') is reduced. The film also removes Ron's defensive aggression in the duel scene and the corridor with Malfoy during Christmas, where his emotional volatility (lunging at Malfoy) is present but contextually thinned. His spontaneous intellectual contributions — working through the Flamel mystery, strategising about Norbert and Charlie — are shared or shortened. His voice is broadly correct but the insecurity register, which is foundational to who book-Ron is, is largely absent.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main traits are present and recognisable: loyalty, humour, bluntness, warmth, bravery. The film earns a solid score in this range. However, the repeated, textured pattern of insecurity about his family's poverty and his standing in the shadow of his brothers is a defining book trait — confirmed structurally by the Mirror of Erised — and it is substantially absent from the film. This is not compression of a single scene; it is the loss of a recurring emotional pattern. This warrants a moderate penalty, keeping the score out of the 23–25 range.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Ron serves several distinct narrative functions in the books: he is Harry's primary emotional anchor and the character who domesticates the magical world for Harry (and the reader); he contributes active problem-solving (identifying Norbert's breed, the Charlie plan, the Flamel Chocolate Frog card discovery alongside Harry, his chess strategy); he is a co-investigator of the Snape/Stone mystery; he provides moral and emotional support during Harry's social ostracism after losing house points; he initiates the plan to get Norbert to Charlie; he acts bravely under pressure in the chess chamber. His agency is consistently meaningful — he is not just Harry's sidekick but an active participant who changes events.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Ron's most prominent act of agency: the chess sacrifice in the underground chamber, which is rendered faithfully and emotionally effectively. He correctly identifies Norbert as a Norwegian Ridgeback. He recognises the invisibility cloak for what it is. He participates actively in the troll confrontation (yelling 'pea brain,' then casting Wingardium Leviosa). He voices concerns and opinions throughout. He contributes to the trio's investigation discussions.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several specific acts of book agency are removed, transferred, or diminished. The Flamel discovery: in the books, it is Harry who notices the Chocolate Frog card and reads the Dumbledore biography, then tells Ron and Hermione — Ron contributes to the subsequent library search, and the find is collaborative. In the film, this is handed largely to Hermione (she produces the book, makes the announcement, explains everything). Ron's role in the Norbert-to-Charlie plan is reduced: in the books he actively proposes this ('Charlie — your brother, Charlie. In Romania') after Harry's prompt; the film gives Ron the identification of the breed but the plan itself is less clearly Ron's initiative. Ron's parallel role in the post-detention social ostracism arc is completely cut (his loyal presence when Harry is shunned by all of Gryffindor, offering comfort and perspective). The scene in which Ron stands by Harry during his social exile ('Only Ron stood by him') is absent. His role as investigative partner — pressing for library searches, engaging with the Snape theory — is present but reduced, with Hermione taking a proportionally larger share of the intellectual agency.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Ron's single most important act of agency — the chess sacrifice — is faithfully preserved and well-staged. His participation in the troll scene is preserved. However, several subsidiary acts of agency are transferred to Hermione or reduced in scope. The loss of his role as Harry's loyal companion during social ostracism removes a meaningful narrative function. The pattern of transfer and reduction is consistent enough to warrant a moderate penalty, but not severe, since his primary heroic act is intact.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Ron's core motivations in Book 1 are: (1) to prove himself as an individual distinct from his high-achieving brothers; (2) loyalty to Harry, rooted partly in genuine affection and partly in the social excitement of being close to someone famous; (3) a desire to belong and be valued, shaped by years of being the youngest, least-noticed Weasley son. His internal conflict is specifically between wanting to be recognised and fearing he never will be — the Mirror of Erised makes this explicit. He is also occasionally driven by resentment (of Hermione's competence, of Malfoy's wealth) that he doesn't fully suppress.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film retains Ron's loyalty to Harry as his primary motivation — this is consistent throughout. His bravery in the chess chamber is explicitly motivated by wanting to stop Snape and protect Harry, which is faithful. His competitive relationship with Hermione (snarling at her in Charms, visibly put out when she succeeds) reflects his resentment of being outshone. The film includes the Mirror scene showing him as head boy and Quidditch captain, which directly confirms his core motivation, but this scene is in the non-theatrical cut material and must be excluded per the instructions. Without this scene, the film's articulation of Ron's internal conflict about being overshadowed is limited to indirect signals.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The Mirror of Erised scene is excluded from theatrical scoring. Without it, the film never explicitly names or confirms Ron's deepest insecurity — that he wants to be recognised as 'the best' rather than another Weasley among many. The train scene's extended self-deprecating confession ('I'm the sixth in our family... you never get anything new') is cut. The result is that Ron's motivational depth — the specific anxiety of being perpetually second — is implied by his reactions but never surfaced. The film preserves the surface behaviour (competitive, occasionally resentful, fiercely loyal) but the internal architecture explaining why he behaves this way is largely absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivations are not wrong in the film — they are simply underexplained and compressed to the point where the specific texture of Ron's insecurity becomes invisible. The behaviour is correct but the inner life behind it is barely present. Per the framework, this is 'partially altered, flattened, or underexplained' territory — the motivations are still the same ones, but stripped to the point where they can only be inferred from residual behaviour rather than observed as a pattern.
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for surface behaviour; reasonably inferred for underlying motivation

character_arc.book_baseline: Ron's arc in Book 1 is relatively compressed but real: he begins as a boy defined primarily by his family context and his insecurities (poverty, overshadowing brothers), grows through genuine friendship with Harry and eventually Hermione, demonstrates courage and self-sacrifice in the chess chamber, and ends the year with his first individual recognition — Dumbledore's fifty points specifically for 'the best-played game of chess Hogwarts has seen in many years.' The arc is from anonymity within a large family to individual recognition earned on his own terms. A secondary arc is the reluctant acceptance of Hermione — the girl he called a nightmare becomes a friend.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film preserves the endpoint of Ron's arc: his chess sacrifice is portrayed as a moment of genuine selfless courage, and Dumbledore's public recognition of him in the Great Hall ('to Mr. Ronald Weasley, for the best played game of chess that Hogwarts has seen these many years, 50 points') is included and plays well. His acceptance of Hermione is also preserved at the end. Ron's surprised, pleased reaction to the points award is in the film.
character_arc.difference: The arc's starting point — Ron's specific insecurity about being overshadowed and unrecognised — is substantially compressed. Without the train's extended conversation about his brothers, without the Remembrall / Christmas / chess-set scenes that accumulate his background, and without the Mirror of Erised confirmation of his deepest desire, the arc's emotional journey is truncated. The audience sees a boy who performs a brave act and gets recognised, but not as clearly the boy for whom recognition was the deepest unmet need. The Hermione reconciliation arc (born of Ron's cruelty, guilt, and the troll moment) is also weakened: the 'birth of the Golden Trio' scene after the troll is cut from theatrical release, removing the explicit emotional reconciliation beat.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc exists and its endpoint is faithfully rendered. However, the starting point is substantially compressed, and two key steps — the texture of his insecurity and the explicit Hermione reconciliation — are absent or cut. This is 'compressed but still faithful' at best, with notable missing steps. The arc is readable but thinner than in the books.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Ron's two primary relationships in Book 1 are: (1) Harry — a friendship of equals built on genuine mutual curiosity, shared adventure, complementary skills, and a specific emotional warmth; Ron is Harry's first real friend and the relationship is reciprocal, not just support-giving. (2) Hermione — initially hostile (snobbish/bossy vs. scruffy/insecure), evolving through the troll incident into the beginning of genuine friendship. Ron's relationship with his family — particularly the weight of his brothers' reputations — is a third important dynamic.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Ron friendship is preserved in its warmth and mutuality. The film shows them bonding on the train, moving through the school together, sharing dangers, and supporting each other. The Hermione dynamic is present: Ron's initial hostility, his public cruelty ('she's a nightmare'), and his eventual side-by-side friendship by the end of the year are all represented. The Weasley family dynamic is touched on briefly (Molly on the platform, Percy in the film, Fred and George) but the specific weight of Ron's brothers as sources of anxiety is largely absent.
key_relationships.difference: The Harry-Ron friendship loses some of its texture: the extended train conversation — in which both boys discover they find each other equally interesting, share insecurities, and build genuine rapport — is compressed into a much shorter exchange. The 'Harry found Ron just as interesting as Ron found him' reciprocity is not emphasised. More significantly, the Hermione reconciliation — the moment that formally seals the Golden Trio — is cut from theatrical release (the 'that's what friends are for' scene). The film shows Ron and Hermione coexisting after the troll but without the explicit emotional beat that marks the shift. Ron's relationship with his family, which defines much of his psychological landscape, is present only superficially in the film.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The core dynamics are present and recognisable. The Harry-Ron friendship functions correctly. The Hermione relationship arc reaches its correct endpoint. However, the theatrical cut of the troll reconciliation scene removes the key beat that makes the Hermione friendship explicit, and the family dynamic is substantially thinner than in the books. This is 'mostly faithful, with some compression or simplification' — but the missing theatrical reconciliation scene is a real loss.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Book Ron is rich with small contradictions and textures: he is simultaneously generous (defending Neville, sharing the world of magic with Harry) and casually cruel (the Hermione comment); brave and cowardly (terrified of spiders, terrified of the dark corridor, but standing his ground); proud and deeply insecure; fiercely loyal but capable of jealousy. The books accumulate dozens of small moments — the bitten hand from Norbert, the chess set that knows him well, the Christmas morning with the maroon sweater, the post-detention social ostracism arc, the Quidditch match where he sits with painted banners for Harry — that build a specific texture of who Ron is as a person and friend. The Mirror of Erised scene confirms his deepest psychological complexity: the desire to be seen as an individual of worth.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film captures Ron's broad strokes: his humour, his loyalty, his bravery in a crisis. Individual moments of nuance are preserved selectively — his blurt about 'killing us faster,' his sarcastic 'lucky we didn't panic,' his pride in his chess sacrifice. His casual cruelty to Hermione and subsequent discomfort when she's hurt are present. The Quidditch match gives him a loyal supporting role.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: A significant amount of accumulative texture is lost. The Norbert arc — Ron's bitten hand, his hospital visit, Malfoy threatening him, his fear alongside determination — is largely cut from the film, removing a sequence that showed Ron at his most simultaneously comic and courageous. The social ostracism arc is entirely absent. The Christmas sequence is trimmed (the maroon sweater exchange, the wizard chess teaching, the extended gift-opening) so that the warmth of Ron's family life and his own mixed feelings about it are not conveyed. The Mirror of Erised theatrical exclusion removes the single scene that makes Ron's complexity most explicit. The Hermione reconciliation cut removes the nuance of Ron's guilt and growth. What remains is a simplified Ron: funny, brave, loyal, occasionally prickly — but without the layered insecurity, the accumulative warmth, and the self-awareness that make book Ron a fully realised character.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The film preserves the outline of Ron but loses a substantial portion of the material that gives him depth. The losses are not isolated — they are systematic: the insecurity texture, the family relationship complexity, the Hermione reconciliation, the Norbert sequence, the ostracism arc, and the Mirror confirmation are all absent or reduced. This is 'noticeable simplification; important nuances, relationships, agency, or contradictions are missing' — warranting a score in the 8–10 range.

score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score above 75 if a core book function, decision, or act of agency is transferred to another character): The Flamel discovery and explanation is substantially transferred to Hermione in the film. Cap enforced — score held at or below 75.

Cap 1 (score above 85 if films remove a major part of complexity, agency, or narrative function): The Mirror of Erised exclusion, the social ostracism arc, and the systematic removal of insecurity texture constitute removal of a major part of Ron's complexity. key_observations: The film's Ron Weasley is recognisable and largely likeable — his loyalty, humour, bravery, and bluntness are all present and consistently rendered. The chess sacrifice, his most important single act in the book, is faithfully preserved and emotionally effective. However, the film loses the character's defining psychological layer: the persistent, low-grade insecurity of being the sixth Weasley son, always overshadowed, always second. This texture is built across dozens of small book moments and confirmed structurally by the Mirror of Erised scene (theatrically excluded). Without it, film-Ron becomes a simpler figure — funny and brave, but missing the internal conflict that makes his eventual recognition by Dumbledore genuinely earned. Additional losses — the social ostracism arc, the Hermione reconciliation, the Norbert sequence detail, and the systematic transfer of intellectual agency to Hermione — compound this simplification. The result is a portrayal that captures Ron's surface correctly but leaves his depth largely unexplored.
